questions.q: What does the honeybee do about the thorns it meets on its way to a flower?
options: It waits for them to be removed
Not quite. The article says: It skilfully avoids them and stays wholly focused on gathering nectar.
It skilfully avoids them and stays wholly focused on gathering nectar
Yes. A lesson in keeping to one’s purpose and rising above bitterness.
It attacks them
Not quite. The article says: It skilfully avoids them and stays wholly focused on gathering nectar.
It gives up and returns to the hive
Not quite. The article says: It skilfully avoids them and stays wholly focused on gathering nectar.
questions.rationale: “Along its journey, the honeybee encounters many thorns. Yet, with skill and determination, it avoids them and alights gently on its intended bloom.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, are provoking and unpleasant experiences needed for spiritual growth?
options: They have no purpose
Not quite. The article says: Calm situations cannot show our patience or compassion; only provocation reveals and builds them.
Calm situations cannot show our patience or compassion; only provocation reveals and builds them
Right. They are tests of character, not random obstacles.
They are punishments for past faults
Not quite. The article says: Calm situations cannot show our patience or compassion; only provocation reveals and builds them.
They make us tougher than other people
Not quite. The article says: Calm situations cannot show our patience or compassion; only provocation reveals and builds them.
questions.rationale: “Calm, untroubled situations cannot reveal our depth of patience or compassion; only extraordinary and provocative moments can do so.”

questions.q: What does “a sound heart” (Quran 26:89) mean, as the article explains it?
options: An uncorrupted inner self – a mind freed by honest introspection from false values and prejudice
Yes. It is the fruit of sustained struggle.
A heart that follows its surroundings
Not quite. The article says: An uncorrupted inner self – a mind freed by honest introspection from false values and prejudice.
A heart that feels no emotion
Not quite. The article says: An uncorrupted inner self – a mind freed by honest introspection from false values and prejudice.
A physically healthy heart
Not quite. The article says: An uncorrupted inner self – a mind freed by honest introspection from false values and prejudice.
questions.rationale: “‘Heart’ does not refer to the physical organ… it signifies the psyche—the inner self that governs thought, intention, and action.”

questions.q: Which two principles does the article place at the core of non-violent social change?
options: Law and punishment
Not quite. The article says: Tolerance and avoidance.
Wealth and influence
Not quite. The article says: Tolerance and avoidance.
Tolerance and avoidance
Well read. “Be tolerant; enjoin what is right; and avoid the ignorant.”
Protest and pressure
Not quite. The article says: Tolerance and avoidance.
questions.rationale: “Two principles form the core of such transformation: tolerance and avoidance.”

questions.article: The Sublime Character of the Prophet
questions.q: Asked about the Prophet’s character, Aishah replied, “Have you not read the Quran?” What did she mean?
options: His character could not be described
Not quite. The article says: His life was the Quran in practice – his words and actions were fully consistent.
He recited it all day
Not quite. The article says: His life was the Quran in practice – his words and actions were fully consistent.
His life was the Quran in practice – his words and actions were fully consistent
Correct. He demonstrated every teaching in his own conduct.
He had written the Quran
Not quite. The article says: His life was the Quran in practice – his words and actions were fully consistent.
questions.rationale: “He was a personification of the Quran. While the Quran presents divine guidance in words, the Prophet’s life was its embodiment.”

questions.article: The Sublime Character of the Prophet
questions.q: When Companions urged him to curse those who had wounded him at Uhud, what did the Prophet answer?
options: “I will leave them to my Companions”
Not quite. The article says: “I have not been sent as a curse… but as a bearer of God’s mercy”.
“Let them be punished tomorrow”
Not quite. The article says: “I have not been sent as a curse… but as a bearer of God’s mercy”.
“I have not been sent as a curse… but as a bearer of God’s mercy”
Yes. He never sought revenge.
He said nothing
Not quite. The article says: “I have not been sent as a curse… but as a bearer of God’s mercy”.
questions.rationale: “I have not been sent as a curse. I have been sent as a proclaimer of Truth and the bearer of God’s mercy.”

questions.q: What does the article identify as the real problem behind communal disputes that are given a religious colour?
options: The political exploitation of religion, not religion itself
Right. Rejecting religion altogether is another extreme.
The existence of several communities
Not quite. The article says: The political exploitation of religion, not religion itself.
Too little political activity
Not quite. The article says: The political exploitation of religion, not religion itself.
Religion as such
Not quite. The article says: The political exploitation of religion, not religion itself.
questions.rationale: “In itself, religion is not the problem. The real problem is the political exploitation of religion by certain individuals and groups.”

questions.article: The World Is Not a Typewriter
questions.q: A man typed “I am right; everyone else is wrong” and felt satisfied. What is the article’s point?
options: Writing is a waste of time
Not quite. The article says: Words on paper come easily, but results in the real world require effort, discipline and readiness to change oneself.
Confidence is all one needs
Not quite. The article says: Words on paper come easily, but results in the real world require effort, discipline and readiness to change oneself.
Typewriters are out of date
Not quite. The article says: Words on paper come easily, but results in the real world require effort, discipline and readiness to change oneself.
Words on paper come easily, but results in the real world require effort, discipline and readiness to change oneself
Yes. Words must be backed by character and work.
questions.rationale: “In the realm of reality, success demands much more than pressing keys. It requires persistent effort… and the willingness to change oneself in accordance with truth.”

questions.q: What does the Prophet’s prayer “show me things as they are” ask for, and what stands in its way?
options: A sharper memory – blocked by age
Not quite. The article says: Objective, as-it-is thinking – which is obscured by the conditioning of one’s upbringing and surroundings.
Faster decisions – blocked by caution
Not quite. The article says: Objective, as-it-is thinking – which is obscured by the conditioning of one’s upbringing and surroundings.
Objective, as-it-is thinking – which is obscured by the conditioning of one’s upbringing and surroundings
Exactly. Deconditioning takes deliberate effort.
More information – blocked by poor schooling
Not quite. The article says: Objective, as-it-is thinking – which is obscured by the conditioning of one’s upbringing and surroundings.
questions.rationale: “He must strive to lift himself to the level of as-it-is thinking—perceiving reality free from the distortions of bias, inherited notions, or group loyalties.”

questions.q: A boy ran away from home at thirteen and returned twelve years later. How does he now look back on those restless years?
options: As preparation – each hardship and mistake taught him resilience, reflection and humility
Well read. “God allowed him to stumble but never to be lost.”
As someone else’s fault
Not quite. The article says: As preparation – each hardship and mistake taught him resilience, reflection and humility.
As wasted time
Not quite. The article says: As preparation – each hardship and mistake taught him resilience, reflection and humility.
As the happiest years of his life
Not quite. The article says: As preparation – each hardship and mistake taught him resilience, reflection and humility.
questions.rationale: “Looking back, he sees those restless years as preparation. Every hardship, every mistake, and every journey taught him resilience, reflection, and humility.”
